summary:
I found the needle and fixed it, but running `test.sh` in this shell hits an environment permission wall unrelated to the fix.

**The bug:** `/app/Dockerfile` assembled `chain.pem` as `cat leaf.crt root.crt intermediate.crt` — the intermediate and root were swapped. `tls.X509KeyPair` correctly puts the leaf at `Certificate[0]` (matching the private key) but preserves the rest in file order, so the server sent the chain `[leaf, root, intermediate]` instead of RFC 5246's required `[leaf, intermediate, root]`. Lenient clients (curl, Go, browsers) tolerate this via graph-based validation; strict sequential validators reject it.

**The fix** (`app/tlssetup/loader.go`): after `X509KeyPair` loads the certs, a new `orderChain` function reorders everything after the leaf by following issuer→subject links, so the chain sent over the wire is always correctly ordered regardless of how the source PEM bundle lists them. I also corrected the Dockerfile's `cat` order for good measure, though the code fix alone is sufficient (and is robust to any future misordering).

I verified the `orderChain` logic directly against the real certs in `/certs/*.crt` (all world-readable): fed it the actual buggy order `[leaf, root, intermediate]` and confirmed it produces `[leaf, intermediate, root]` with each cert's issuer matching the next cert's subject — exactly what `test.sh`'s chain-order check requires. `go vet` also passes cleanly.

I couldn't get `test.sh` itself to run end-to-end here: my shell is an unprivileged user (`bench`, uid 1001, zero effective capabilities), while `test.sh` needs to write the built binary to `/usr/local/bin` (root-owned, mode 755) and read `/certs/leaf.key` (root-owned, mode 600). Both fail with `permission denied` before the actual TLS/chain logic is ever exercised — this is a pre-existing environment restriction, not something introduced by my change. If you can run `test.sh` as root (or in the container's default context), it should now pass; happy to help further if it doesn't.
